compiled_state.description:
# A dedicated `parent` verb, with `--force`

Raised while repairing an incident (88d9-fe42-e50f-4067) in which a reconcile pass cleared the
`parent_id` of 63 tickets. Every prior parent was recoverable from the event log, but rebar had **no
supported way to write most of them back**. Filed as an idea by operator direction: out of scope for
that session.

## The gap

Hierarchy is edited only as a side effect of `edit`:

* `edit --parent` is the ONLY reparent path. There is no `parent` / `move` / `reparent` verb, and
  `link`/`unlink` cover the six link RELATIONS, not containment.
* `edit` has no `--force`, so the `--parent` cascade's refusal
  (`_commands/composer.py:503-513`, "cannot re-parent to closed ticket") is absolute.
* `rebar revert <ticket> <uuid>` does not help: `process_revert`
  (`reducer/_processors.py:456-488`) only appends to `state["reverts"]`; its sole state effect is
  un-archiving on REVERT-of-ARCHIVED. Reverting the offending EDIT leaves `parent_id` empty.
* `fsck-recover` is git-level dangling-write recovery, not semantic repair.
* `rebar.edit_ticket` shells out to the same CLI, so the library inherits the guard.

Net: the reconciler can DESTROY a parent edge automatically, but an operator cannot RESTORE one when
the parent is closed — and the store has no supported route back to a state it previously held. The
documented workaround ("reopen the parent first") means, at incident scale, reopening ~20 epics and
re-closing them, which re-runs the LLM completion gate on already-signed closes and risks leaving a
previously-closed epic open.

In this incident 61 of 63 affected tickets were closed and the current state was ACCEPTED by the
operator on that basis; only the two non-closed tickets were repaired, and they were repairable
precisely because their parents were still `open` / `in_progress`.

## Shape

A first-class `parent` verb owning containment, rather than a field on `edit`:

    rebar parent <child> <parent> [--force]
    rebar parent <child> --detach

with `--force` scoped to bypass ONLY a positively-known closed/inactive parent. Deliberately still
enforced under `--force`: the parent must exist, no self-parent, no cycle, and the fail-closed branch
for an UNVERIFIABLE status (`--force` overrides a KNOWN-closed parent, never an UNKNOWN one). Follows
rebar's existing idiom (`claim --force`, `transition --force-close`): explicit intent, audited, never
implicit.

Worth considering alongside it: whether `--force` should require a reason string (as `--force-close`
does) so a hierarchy override leaves the same audit quality as a gate override.

## Why an idea rather than a bug

The capability gap is real but it only bites during repair of a defect that should not recur — the
inbound parent clear that caused this incident was reverted, and its root cause (deciding a peer
deletion from `managed_refs`, which cannot prove the peer ever had the ref) is being fixed separately.
So this is a resilience/ergonomics improvement to reach for deliberately, not an urgent fix.
compiled_state.title: Add a dedicated parent verb with --force, so a destroyed hierarchy is repairable
